en: "Having made [the thought] 'this is the vajra' means: having ascertained that 'this very mind of mine has the form of the moon-vajra of all the Tathāgatas,' one should cause those Buddhas in the form of moon-vajras to enter the armor which consists of the three bodies (*trikāya*); this is the meaning. By such meditation, those who accomplish rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*) and so forth become well-protected.
*Vajraratna* is the bliss of indivisible protection; by means of that, in the wheel-mandala (*cakramaṇḍala*), an illumination (*uddyota*) is produced, and thus it is so called. || O ||

[Furthermore, in this very context: "Space-vajra," and so forth. In the center of the lotus-sun seat situated within the mind-maṇḍala inside Māmakī’s white lotus, one should visualize oneself as Akṣobhya—born from the syllable *raṃ*, seated upon a blazing triangular *repha* mark, and established within the fire-maṇḍala—just like Mahāvajradhara. One should then visualize the object of practice (the *sādhya*) as having accumulated defilements, with his mouth opened wide, overwhelmed by fear, standing before one in the fire-maṇḍala, naked, stripped of armor, and his body smeared with oil.

One should meditate that the sky-element is filled with various jackals, crows, vultures, and dogs, and with fierce, violent, and wrathful Vajra-rākṣasas emerging from the mouths of rays of light produced by the *ālambā* and *svarosatka*; and that [the victim] is attacked and torn into pieces by these wrathful ones who wield various weapons, while their entrails, marrow, and so forth are torn out and devoured by the rākṣasas and others.

By the words "Buddha" and so forth: even one who meditates on [himself as] a Buddha or other [deities], having had his mouth opened and closed [by the enemy], will certainly die within a fortnight by means of this meditation, even if its excellence has not yet been attained, provided it is applied [correctly].
This refers to the malevolent rite (*abhicāra*) performed by Vajrarākṣasa and others.

In the fourteenth [chapter], beginning with "Then," and so forth: *kāya* is Vairocana; his manifestation is the *kāyavijṛmbhita*, which consists of the mantra and so on. That which is indivisible from that is what is so described. Through union with that, the *kāyasamaya*—Vairocana—is impelled. The mantra by which he himself is impelled and fixed as a stake (*kīla*) is what he emitted from the vajras of body, speech, and mind. "One should not bind hand-mudrās if one desires the supreme accomplishment"—since this has been stated right here, it is for the sake of the supreme practice (*uttamasādhana*); therefore, it is said.

"Mutual entwining" means that through the yoga of Vairocana, together with a vajra-maiden visualized as Ārya-Locanā and so forth, there is mutual embracing and so on; this is the form of mutual entwining.
"The thumb" refers to one's own blazing secret vajra. "The foot" is the place of great bliss known as the *dharmodayā*; the union of these two is the "closing of the thumb and the foot.
"The striking down of the vajra-stake" means this: [the following].
Possessing the yoga of the blazing and fierce Vairocana together with all his black vidyās as they truly are, he stands upon his own vidyā-lotus within the fiery maṇḍala.

"It should be stated that it is preceded by Vajra": *vajrārka* is simply the sun (*arka*). When that has set, "he who is the initiator of the practice"—that is, at the time of the rising of the *araṇa*, which is the driver of the sun’s chariot—he achieves success within seven days. However, for one who is always established in yoga, because there is no restriction of time, it is stated otherwise: because he possesses the dawn of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that gathers in all sentient beings and because he dispels the darkness of ignorance, his own secret vajra itself is the sun; thus, it is *vajrārka*.

When that has set and the woman—the *svadhātu*—has disappeared, the *bodhicitta* is "without conflict" (*araṇa*); its arising is its emission. By this, the following would be stated: one who always possesses the yoga of the deity-ego, having entered into union with the deity of his own family, performing the radiation and so forth, slightly moving [the organ] while not emitting the *bodhicitta*, and meditating, will certainly [attain realization] at the very moment of the arising of the *sambodhicitta*, by virtue of the flavor of being absorbed in that; such is the meaning. And it is said:
"As long as the yogi does not perform the emission of the *bodhicitta*..."
At that moment, one attains an uninterrupted, indescribable bliss born of bliss— a sudden flash of form that expands and withdraws,
illuminating this entire universe of Bhūr, Bhuvas, and Svar, including all things moving and stationary.
From tasting the flavor of its own intrinsic nature, that which is beyond the senses is attained;
even by the Buddhas, it cannot be said, "This is that.
It is eternal, all-pervading, supreme, peaceful, and devoid of causes and examples.
The supreme state is free from existence and non-existence and beyond all dualities. When this bodhicitta, the treasury of all accomplishments, has fallen away,
and when the aggregates and consciousness have fainted, how can there be any irreproachable accomplishment?

Furthermore, in this very context: "the space-element" (*khadhātu*) refers here to the space-element (*ākāśadhātu*). "Of the complete one" means filled with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. "Destroyed by that wicked one" means one should meditate on him having been cut and pulverized by that [wicked one] holding an axe and a mallet in his hands. "At that very moment" means that immediately after being joined to the meditation being explained, even one equal to Vajrasattva dies; such is the meaning. "One should contemplate," etc., refers to the enemy who harms all Buddhas.

Having killed the Buddhas and others, he becomes filled with remorse, terrified, and overwhelmed by fear. Distraught by the dread of falling into hell, without refuge or protection, naked, his armor stripped away, and his body smeared with oil—having visualized him thus, opened by means of the previously mentioned sequence of the *saṃpuṭa*, and placed within the fire mandala; then, for his very benefit, the practitioner endowed with the yoga of the wrathful deity named Amṛta, stationed in the midst of the circle of deities of the maṇḍala who have entered the essence of wrath, [should act] through the emanations of Rākṣasas and so forth...
"By means of the mantra" means that which is indivisible by means of the mantra. "Entering" means that one should thus apply the *vyāna* [breath].

In the seventeenth [chapter], wisdom (*prajñā*)—which has the form of penetrating all phenomena like space—is expressed by the term "space-vajra" (*khavajra*). The "element-commitment" (*dhātusamaya*) is the Great Bliss Vajra (*mahāsukhavajra*), because it is not to be transgressed for the sake of the arising of perfect awakening. "That very same" means that very wisdom just mentioned is the vajra; for there is the statement: "Pure intellect, resembling the moon, is designated as 'vajra'."

He who holds her—who has assumed the form of Samantabhadra—by means of the union of embracing through meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), is Vajradhara, the glorious Great Bliss (*Śrīmahāsukha*). By this [description], he is surrounded by the four goddesses, Locanā and the others, whose intrinsic nature consists of the elements such as earth; he is the one who penetrates all phenomena (*sarvadharmaprativedhyaka*). Having attained the state of Samantabhadra, the glorious Great Bliss is composed of the five secrets.

The "worlds" (*bhuvana*) of all the Tathāgatas are the lotuses of Locanā and the others. He is the Lord (*īśvara*) over them because of being joined with the meditative absorption of union with them. Thus, the glorious Vajrasattva is the Lord of the worlds of all the Tathāgatas.
Likewise, in this very [text]: "In the center of the space-element... and so forth.
